name: Benny Goodman
aliases: Benjamin David Goodman; King of Swing
description: Benny Goodman, born Benjamin David Goodman on May 30, 1909, in Chicago's Maxwell Street neighborhood, was an American clarinetist and bandleader known as the King of Swing. The ninth of twelve children of Jewish immigrants David and Dora Goodman, he learned clarinet at Kehelah Jacob Synagogue and in the Hull House band, was working professionally by 1921, and held a union card at thirteen. He joined Ben Pollack's orchestra at sixteen and made his first recordings in 1926. After freelance work in New York from 1929, he formed his own orchestra in 1934, broadcast on NBC's Let's Dance with arrangements by Fletcher Henderson, and opened at Los Angeles's Palomar Ballroom on August 21, 1935 — the engagement remembered as the symbolic start of the Swing Era. His January 16, 1938, Carnegie Hall concert brought jazz to that stage as headline art. Goodman died on June 13, 1986, in New York City.

name: Blueface
description: Blueface, born Johnathan Porter on 20 January 1997 in Los Angeles, California, is an American rapper. A former high-school and college football player, he turned to rap in 2017 and broke virally with the "Respect My Cryppin'" video in October 2018, noted for his offbeat flow. He signed to Cash Money West in November 2018, and "Thotiana" (2018) became his signature hit, peaking at No. 8 on the Billboard Hot 100 after Cardi B and YG remixes. His mixtape Famous Cryp (2018) preceded the debut studio album Find the Beat (2020), and he was named to the 2019 XXL Freshman Class. He pleaded guilty in the October 2022 Las Vegas shooting case and received three years' probation in October 2023; a probation violation brought a four-year sentence in August 2024, and he was released from prison in November 2025.

name: BabyChiefDoit
aliases: Jayden Whitter Jones; Jayden Whittier Jones
description: BabyChiefDoit is an American drill rapper from Chicago's South Side, born circa 2008, whose rise made him one of the youngest charting figures in Chicago rap. Signed to Artist Partner Group (APG), he broke through in 2024 with "Pancakes & Drugs" and "6ix Times 2Day"; "Rollin" entered the TikTok Billboard Top 50. His albums are Animals Only (2024) and Zoo Life (23 April 2025), and he was named to the 2025 XXL Freshman Class. "Went West" (2025) became his first Billboard Hot 100 entry, peaking at No. 71 in July 2025. He has performed at Chicago's Lyrical Lemonade Summer Smash and Rolling Loud, was featured on Chance the Rapper's "Drapetomania" (2025), and drew wide coverage in August 2025 for stating in a Power 105.1 interview that he used ChatGPT to help write lyrics. His exact birth date and the spelling of his legal name remain unresolved in authoritative sources and are not asserted.

name: Big Boy
description: Big Boy, born Kurt Alexander on 8 September 1969 in Chicago, Illinois, is an American radio host — not Antwan "Big Boi" Patton of Outkast, a different person with a near-identical billing, from whom this record is expressly distinguished. He moved to California at age two and, after work as a bodyguard for The Pharcyde, began in radio in 1994 at KPWR (Power 106), Los Angeles. He launched the morning show Big Boy's Neighborhood on Power 106 in 1997; syndicated nationally from 2007, it was heard in 35 major markets at its peak. He moved the show to KRRL (Real 92.3) in February 2015 and was inducted into the Radio Hall of Fame the same year; he received the 2,701st star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame in 2021 and, per spring 2026 Nielsen reporting, currently hosts on Real 92.3.

name: Boosie Badazz
aliases: Torrence Ivy Hatch Jr.; Lil Boosie; Lil' Boosie
description: Boosie Badazz, born 14 November 1982 in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, is an American rapper formerly billed as Lil Boosie. He joined the Baton Rouge collective Concentration Camp in the late 1990s, debuted solo with Youngest of da Camp (2000), and signed to Pimp C's Trill Entertainment for For My Thugz (2002). His mainstream breakthrough Bad Azz (2006) included "Zoom." Acquitted of first-degree murder in 2012, he was released from prison on 5 March 2014 after serving about five years on drug charges, and adopted the Boosie Badazz name. Touch Down 2 Cause Hell (2015) peaked at No. 3 on the Billboard 200. The spelling of his legal name is contested across sources — "Torrence Ivy Hatch Jr." in Wikipedia's infobox, "Torence" in its lead — and is carried here as a documented variant, not a settled fact.

name: Bronze Thrills
description: Bronze Thrills was a Black-audience true-story magazine published in Fort Worth, Texas, by the Good Publishing Company, the house behind Sepia. The title began as a renaming: Horace J. Blackwell had founded The World's Messenger in 1942, and after George Levitan bought Blackwell's magazines and the Good Publishing Company in 1950, he changed the Messenger's name to Bronze Thrills and, in the standard account of the company, had success with it for some time. Surviving issues present the magazine as a confessional true-story monthly for Black women readers: the November 1959 issue (Volume 8, Number 11) carries the cover line "America's Greatest Negro True Story Magazine" and first-person stories of love, marriage, crime, and repentance, with advice columns and household features. A digitized November 1976 issue (Volume 25, Number 11) survives at the Internet Archive, and issues dated as late as June 1982 are documented in the collectors' market, giving the magazine a run of roughly three decades alongside Sepia, Hep, and Jive in the Good Publishing stable.

name: Birmingham Black Barons
description: The Birmingham Black Barons were a Negro leagues baseball club based in Birmingham, Alabama, that played from 1920 to 1960 and shared Rickwood Field with the white Birmingham Barons on alternating stands. The National Park Service's Rickwood Field nomination records the Black Barons as charter members of the Negro Southern League of 1920, and the club later played in the Negro National League before joining the newly formed Negro American League in 1937. Sources differ on the club's pennant count, and this record does not blend them: the National Park Service nomination credits Negro American League pennants in 1943 and 1948, while Birmingham and league histories count three pennants, adding 1944. The 1948 club, a pennant winner under either count, carried the seventeen-year-old outfielder Willie Mays and lost the final Negro World Series to the Homestead Grays. Earlier Black Barons included Satchel Paige and Mule Suttles, both named in the National Park Service nomination. As the major leagues integrated after 1947, Black Barons including Dan Bankhead and Piper Davis crossed to major-league organizations, and the club played its last game in 1960.

name: Barstool Sports
description: Barstool Sports is an American digital media company founded by Dave Portnoy in 2003 as a free print publication distributed to Boston-area commuters, offering sports commentary and gambling content, before growing into a website and a podcast-led media business. In January 2020 PENN Entertainment bought a minority stake of about 36 percent for 163 million dollars, and by February 2023 PENN had paid 551 million dollars in total to acquire the whole company. The arrangement lasted months: in August 2023, as PENN moved its sportsbook to an ESPN partnership, it sold 100 percent of Barstool back to Portnoy for one dollar, with non-compete covenants and a right to half of the gross proceeds of any future sale. In Black sports-and-culture media, Barstool's documented place in this graph is its podcast era with 'Million Dollaz Worth of Game' (CTL-E-5569): the Philadelphia show hosted by Gillie Da King and Wallo267 signed with Barstool in 2020 in a deal reported at three million dollars for a fifty percent stake, and signed a new contract with the company in 2022.

name: Black Liberation Army
description: The Black Liberation Army (BLA) was an underground organization in the United States active from 1970 to 1981. Reference accounts describe it as a Marxist–Leninist, Black nationalist organization composed largely of former members of the Black Panther Party, together with members of the Republic of New Afrika, who had worked above ground before going underground amid the Black Panther Party's internal split of the early 1970s. Its stated goal, in its own program's terms, was to take up arms for the liberation and self-determination of Black people in the United States, and its program was one of war against the United States government. The actions attributed to the organization in the historical record include bombings, killings of police officers, robberies — termed 'expropriations' by participants — and prison breaks. Its most documented individual case is that of Assata Shakur (CTL-E-5693): the Associated Press describes her as a member of both the Black Panther Party and the Black Liberation Army, convicted in 1977 in the 1973 New Jersey Turnpike shootout, who escaped prison in 1979 and lived in Cuba until her death in 2025. The organization was inactive after 1981.

name: Blackwatch
aliases: Blackwatch Movement; The Blackwatch Movement; Black Watch Movement
description: Blackwatch — usually styled the Blackwatch Movement — is the Brooklyn Black-nationalist movement and artist collective that stood behind X-Clan and gave hip-hop's Afrocentric wave an organizational home. In Professor X's own account, preserved in Brian Coleman's hip-hop history reporting, the Blackwatch crew — including Isis, Unique & Dashan and Queen Mother Rage — existed before X-Clan, and his idea was to make a fan-club base into a movement. The Source's X-Clan histories describe Blackwatch as an organization led by Professor X's father, Brooklyn activist Sonny 'Abubadika' Carson, and credit it with legitimizing X-Clan's involvement in raising the consciousness of the hip-hop generation. X-Clan's own graph record (CTL-E-5676) states the relationship the same way: the group was the best-known component of the Blackwatch Movement, which Professor X helped build and his father led. Blackwatch-affiliated artists released a run of records in the early 1990s, among them Isis's Rebel Soul (1990) and Queen Mother Rage's Vanglorious Law (1991), extending the movement's reach beyond the Clan itself. The surviving documentation is thin and mostly oral-history based, and this record carries only what those sources support.

name: Brother J
aliases: Grand Verbalizer Funkin' Lesson Brother J; Brother J the Grand Verbalizer; Jason Hunter
description: Brother J (born Jason Hunter), billed in full as Grand Verbalizer Funkin' Lesson Brother J, is the lead lyricist and frontman of the Brooklyn hip-hop group X-Clan. AllMusic's artist entry lists him as a member of X Clan, and the group's biographies identify him as one of its primary members, alongside Professor X the Overseer, Paradise the Architect and Sugar Shaft the Rhythm Provider. His instructional, Afrocentric lyricism carried X-Clan's two foundational albums, To the East, Blackwards (1990) and Xodus (1992), including the tracks 'Funkin' Lesson' and 'Heed the Word of the Brother.' After the group's mid-1990s break-up he formed Dark Sun Riders, which released Seeds of Evolution in 1996, and in 2004 he assembled a new lineup under the name X Clan Millennium Cipher. Following Professor X's death in 2006, Brother J led the reformed X-Clan on Return from Mecca (2007) and Mainstream Outlawz (2009), and he remains the leader of the group's current incarnation. In a 2008 Final Call interview tied to a Saviours' Day performance, he described his lyrical aim as speech in service of truth and uplift rather than commercial excess.

name: B.B. King
description: B.B. King, born Riley B. King on 16 September 1925 near Itta Bena, Mississippi, was an American blues guitarist and singer raised in the Mississippi Delta, where gospel singing in church was his earliest musical influence. He developed a lyrical single-string guitar style with a distinctive vibrato, shaped by T-Bone Walker, Delta blues players including his cousin Bukka White, and jazz guitarists Django Reinhardt and Charlie Christian. Working as a disc jockey at WDIA in Memphis, he took the name "B.B.," short for "Blues Boy." His 1951 hit recording of "Three O'Clock Blues" began a lifetime of near-continuous touring — often 300 or more one-night stands a year. In 1964, in Chicago, he recorded the seminal live album Live at the Regal at the Regal Theater on the city's South Side. His 1969 recording "The Thrill Is Gone" won the first of his 15 Grammy Awards, and the guitar he named Lucille became one of the most famous instruments in American music. He was inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 1987. King died on 14 May 2015 in Las Vegas, Nevada, at age 89.

name: Bo Diddley
aliases: Ellas McDaniel; Ellas Otha Bates; The Originator
description: Bo Diddley, born Ellas Otha Bates on December 30, 1928, in McComb, Mississippi, and later known as Ellas McDaniel after his adoptive mother, was an American singer, guitarist, and songwriter raised in Chicago from childhood. Reuters' obituary reporting records that he took the name McDaniel from his adoptive mother, played classical violin as a boy, picked up the nickname Bo Diddley as a teenager after moving to Chicago, and began playing music on Chicago street corners in the 1940s. Britannica notes that he was raised in Chicago and got his stage name while recording for Chicago's Chess Records, the label that released his string of 1950s records beginning with his signature song "Bo Diddley" in 1955. His syncopated signature rhythm — the Bo Diddley beat, with African roots — became, in Britannica's assessment, an irresistible rock and roll dance sound that fellow artists widely adopted, and his experiments with guitar effects and his flamboyant stage shows shaped early rock. NPR's 2008 obituary coverage confirms that Chess Records released his hits after his 1955 breakthrough and that he died of heart failure at his home in Archer, Florida, on June 2, 2008, at the age of 79. He was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1987 and received a Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award in 1998.

name: Be Altitude: Respect Yourself
description: Be Altitude: Respect Yourself is a 1972 soul album by the Staple Singers, released in February 1972 on Stax Records (STS 3002). Craft Recordings, in its 50th Anniversary Edition, describes it as the group's iconic fourth album for Stax. The album was recorded at Muscle Shoals Sound Studios in Muscle Shoals, Alabama, and produced by Al Bell, with the Muscle Shoals Rhythm Section and the Memphis Horns as the backing musicians. Its ten tracks open with 'This World' and include the two songs that carry the album's title and legacy: 'Respect Yourself,' written by Luther Ingram and Mack Rice, and 'I'll Take You There,' written by Alvertis Isbell, which Craft identifies as a Billboard Hot 100 No. 1 hit. The performing group on the record is the family quartet of Roebuck 'Pops' Staples with Cleotha, Mavis and Yvonne Staples. The remaining tracks include 'Name the Missing Word,' 'This Old Town (People in This Town),' 'We the People,' 'Are You Sure,' 'Who Do You Think You Are? (Jesus Christ the Super Star),' 'I'm Just Another Soldier' and 'Who.'

name: Barrett Sisters
aliases: The Barrett Sisters; Barrett and Hudson Singers; Sweet Sisters of Zion
description: The Barrett Sisters were a Chicago gospel trio of sisters DeLois Barrett Campbell (March 12, 1926 – August 2, 2011), Billie Barrett GreenBey (1928–2020) and Rodessa Barrett Porter (1930–2024) — the youngest sister's given name also appears as 'Rhodessa.' Raised on Chicago's South Side, they sang as children in the choir of Morning Star Baptist Church under their aunt, choir director Mattie Dacus, and from 1936 sang locally with a cousin as the Barrett and Hudson Singers; when the cousin died in 1950, Rodessa took her place and the group took the Barrett Sisters name. DeLois sang with the Roberta Martin Singers from her high-school years into the early 1960s, when Roberta Martin encouraged her independent career with her sisters. Their first album, Jesus Loves Me, was released on Savoy Records (dated 1963 in the New York Times account), and they recorded for Creed Records in the 1970s. Featured in the 1982 documentary Say Amen, Somebody, they toured internationally for decades; Chicago Tribune critic Howard Reich called them the greatest female trio in gospel history, and their story is told in the documentary The Sweet Sisters of Zion.

name: Bronny James
aliases: LeBron James Jr.; LeBron Raymone James Jr.
description: Bronny James, born LeBron James Jr. in 2004, is an American professional basketball player for the Los Angeles Lakers and the eldest son of LeBron James. A McDonald's All-American at Sierra Canyon School, he played one season at the University of Southern California, a freshman year delayed after he suffered cardiac arrest during a summer 2023 workout and underwent a procedure for a congenital heart defect; he averaged 4.8 points in 25 games. The Lakers selected him 55th overall in the 2024 NBA draft, and that October he and his father became the first father-son pair to play together in an NBA game. He has developed across his first two seasons between the Lakers and their G League program. In July 2026 his father left Los Angeles for Philadelphia, leaving Bronny as the lone James on the Lakers roster; entering his third season in October 2026, his salary for 2026-27 is fully guaranteed and Los Angeles continues to develop him as a rotation guard.

name: Bessie Smith
description: Bessie Smith, born in Chattanooga, Tennessee, and killed in a car crash near Clarksdale, Mississippi, on September 26, 1937, was the “Empress of the Blues” and the most commanding blues singer of the recording era's first decades. Orphaned young, she sang for pennies on Chattanooga street corners, joined Ma Rainey's orbit about 1912–1913, and signed with Columbia Records in February 1923. Her first coupling, including “Down Hearted Blues,” was a phenomenon, and across roughly 160 Columbia recordings between 1923 and the early 1930s she worked with Fletcher Henderson, Louis Armstrong — their 1925 “St. Louis Blues” is a canonical recording — Benny Goodman, and Coleman Hawkins. Smith headlined the Theater Owners Booking Association circuit and was, by wide agreement, the highest-paid Black entertainer of her time. She was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1989.

name: Bo Jackson
description: Vincent Edward “Bo” Jackson, born 30 November 1962 in Bessemer, Alabama, is an African American athlete widely regarded as the greatest two-sport professional of the modern era. At Auburn he won the 1985 Heisman Trophy while also starring in baseball and track. He debuted in Major League Baseball with the Kansas City Royals in 1986 and simultaneously played running back for the Los Angeles Raiders, splitting four years between the two sports. A hip injury suffered in an NFL playoff game in January 1991 ended his football career, yet he returned to baseball — later with an artificial hip — playing for the Chicago White Sox and California Angels through 1994. In September 2026 the Louisville Slugger Museum named him its 2026 “Living Legend,” with the award ceremony set for 13 November 2026 in Louisville.

name: Barry Bonds
description: Barry Bonds, born Barry Lamar Bonds on 24 July 1964 in Riverside, California, is a Black American former left fielder who holds the most contested records in baseball. The son of outfielder Bobby Bonds and the godson of Willie Mays, he was drafted by the Pittsburgh Pirates in 1985 and debuted on 30 May 1986, winning National League MVP awards in 1990 and 1992 before signing with the San Francisco Giants. Over 22 seasons he set the career home run record with 762, the single-season record with 73 in 2001, and the career walks record with 2,558, while remaining the only player with 500 home runs and 500 stolen bases. He won a record seven MVP awards, fourteen All-Star selections, eight Gold Gloves and twelve Silver Sluggers, and finished with a .298 average and 2,935 hits. Pittsburgh inducted him into its team Hall of Fame in 2024. One adjudicated legal fact is carried in this record: his 2011 obstruction-of-justice conviction was overturned on appeal in 2015.

name: Bill Pickett
aliases: Willie M. Pickett; The Dusky Demon
description: Bill Pickett (1870–1932) was the African American cowboy who originated rodeo steer wrestling, known as bulldogging. The National Cowboy & Western Heritage Museum records that he was born in 1870 in Travis County, Texas, and with four brothers ran the Pickett Brothers Bronco Busters and Rough Riders. His method for subduing a steer — seizing its horns, twisting its head upward and biting its nose or lower lip as bulldogs did with strays — became a rodeo exhibition act by the early 1900s, and in refined form steer wrestling remains a standard rodeo event. Pickett was a featured performer with the Miller Brothers 101 Ranch and Wild West Show for more than a quarter century, billed as the Dusky Demon, and he also appeared in early Black-cast Western films. Excluded from some venues because he was Black, he sometimes performed under a claimed Native identity. He died in 1932 of injuries from a horse at the 101 Ranch. He was inducted into the National Rodeo Hall of Fame, the museum's page dating the induction to 1972.

name: Black Star Line
aliases: Black Star Line, Inc.; The Oceanic Steam Navigation Company (Black Star Line)
description: The Black Star Line was the steamship company Marcus Garvey and fellow members of the Universal Negro Improvement Association incorporated in Delaware in 1919, naming it in deliberate counterpoint to the White Star Line. Financed by five-dollar shares sold at UNIA meetings and through the movement press, it was meant to carry goods and passengers between Black communities in North America, the Caribbean, and Africa, and to stand as visible proof of Black commercial capacity. Its first ship, the Yarmouth, intended for renaming as the Frederick Douglass, sailed with a Black captain and crew, and two further vessels followed in 1920. The enterprise was undermined by overpriced, worn ships, costly repairs, inexperienced management, and federal investigation; operations were suspended in 1922, and Garvey's later mail-fraud conviction grew out of its stock promotion. As a business it failed, but as a symbol of Black economic self-determination it endured far beyond its short operating life.

name: Bobby Hutton
aliases: Robert James Hutton; Lil' Bobby Hutton; Bobby James Hutton
description: Robert James Hutton, known as Bobby or Lil' Bobby Hutton, born 21 April 1950 in Jefferson County, Arkansas, was the first recruit and first treasurer of the Black Panther Party. His family moved to Oakland, California, in 1953, fleeing harassment by Ku Klux Klan-linked nightriders, part of the second Great Migration. In December 1966, at sixteen, Hutton met party founders Huey P. Newton and Bobby Seale at the North Oakland Anti-Poverty Center and became the party's first and youngest member, drawn by its Ten-Point Program. On 2 May 1967 he joined the armed Panther demonstration at the California State Capitol in Sacramento protesting the Mulford Act, and was arrested there and again later that month on firearms charges. On 6 April 1968, two days after Martin Luther King Jr.'s assassination, Hutton was with Eldridge Cleaver and other Panthers in a confrontation with Oakland police in which two officers were wounded; after a ninety-minute gun battle at a West Oakland house, Hutton was shot and killed by police as he emerged. Eldridge Cleaver said Hutton was surrendering; police said he tried to run. He was seventeen, and the party's first member killed.

name: Bayard Rustin
description: Bayard Rustin, born 17 March 1912 in West Chester, Pennsylvania, was an American civil rights organizer, adviser to Martin Luther King Jr., and the chief organizer of the 1963 March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom. Raised by Quaker grandparents, he worked for the Fellowship of Reconciliation from 1941 to 1953 and organized the New York branch of the Congress of Racial Equality. A pacifist, he was imprisoned during World War II as a conscientious objector and in 1947 coordinated the Journey of Reconciliation, a model for the Freedom Rides. In the mid-1950s he became a close adviser to King, helped organize the Southern Christian Leadership Conference. Working with A. Philip Randolph, he directed the logistics of the March on Washington in August 1963, the largest civil rights demonstration of its era. He later led the A. Philip Randolph Institute from 1966 to 1979 and, in the 1980s, spoke publicly for gay rights; his 1953 arrest on a morals charge, for which California pardoned him in 2020, had long pushed him to work behind the scenes. Rustin died on 24 August 1987 in New York. President Barack Obama posthumously awarded him the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2013.

name: Betty Shabazz
description: Betty Shabazz, born Betty Dean Sanders — Britannica gives 28 May 1934, in Pinehurst, Georgia — was an American educator and civil rights advocate, best known as the wife of Malcolm X. Raised in Detroit by foster parents Lorenzo and Helen Malloy, she studied elementary education at Tuskegee Institute, where she first encountered Southern racism directly, then moved to New York and trained as a registered nurse. There she met Malcolm X, joined the Nation of Islam in 1956, and married him in January 1958. The couple left the Nation in 1964. On 21 February 1965, pregnant with twins, she sat with her four daughters in the Audubon Ballroom and witnessed his assassination. Widowed at thirty, she raised six daughters alone while earning bachelor's and master's degrees and, in 1975, a doctorate in higher-education administration from the University of Massachusetts Amherst. At Medgar Evers College in Brooklyn she rose as a professor, administrator and fundraiser, preserving her husband's legacy while building a reputation of her own as a speaker for women, education and human rights. She died in the Bronx on 23 June 1997, of burns suffered in a fire set by her young grandson.

name: Big Time Sarah
aliases: Sarah Streeter; Big Time Sarah and the BTS Express
description: Big Time Sarah, born Sarah Streeter on January 31, 1953 in Coldwater, Mississippi, was an American blues singer raised in Chicago, where she sang in gospel choirs in South Chicago churches. At fourteen she began singing blues at Morgan's Lounge, and in the 1970s she played with musicians including Magic Slim, Buddy Guy, Junior Wells and Sunnyland Slim. Her work with Sunnyland Slim led to her first solo release, a single on his Airway Records label. Teamed with Zora Young and Bonnie Lee as Blues with the Girls, she toured Europe in 1982 and recorded an album in Paris. From 1989 she performed with her own band, the BTS Express, becoming a featured performer in North Side Chicago blues clubs and at blues festivals. She recorded for Chicago's Delmark Records from 1993, releasing Lay It on 'em Girls (1993), Blues in the Year One-D-One (1996) and A Million of You (2001). Big Time Sarah died on June 13, 2015, aged 62, from heart complications in a Chicago-area nursing home.

name: Brooklyn Queen
description: Brooklyn Queen, born 3 July 2005 in Detroit, Michigan, is an American rapper and creator. An African-American artist raised by her mother, the independent rapper Nailnotirious Kim, who named her for Brooklyn, New York, she wrote her first song at five and made her first studio recording at eight. She signed with BMB Entertainment at eleven and made her teenage debut in 2017 with the viral, kid-friendly dance record "Keke Taught Me," followed the same year by her debut album Queens Corner. A bright, dance-friendly spin on trap rap, her early catalogue continued with singles including "Beat the Baby" and, in 2018, "Emoji" and "Feeling So Wavy." She has also acted, playing Senna in Brat TV's Charmers in 2021, and remains an active recording and streaming artist; AllMusic credits 2025 releases including "Twerk It" and "Too Late" featuring Dre Butterz, and she streamed live on TikTok in September 2026.

name: Blac Chyna
description: Angela Renée White, born 11 May 1988 in Washington, D.C., is an American model, television personality and entrepreneur known professionally as Blac Chyna. Working as an exotic dancer in Miami, including at the King of Diamonds club, she rose to prominence in 2010 as Nicki Minaj's stunt double in Kanye West's 'Monster' music video and after Drake name-dropped her in 'Miss Me' that year, leading to covers for Dimepiece, Straight Stuntin and Black Men's Magazine. She trained at JLS Professional Make Up Artist School, launched the online boutique 88fin and, in 2014, her makeup brand Lashed by Blac Chyna and a beauty salon in Encino, Los Angeles. She starred with Rob Kardashian in the E! reality series Rob & Chyna in 2016. From 2022 she publicly returned to using her birth name, Angela White, documenting sobriety, baptism and the reversal of cosmetic procedures, and in 2026 she announced a memoir, Sober Mine.

name: BruceDropEmOff
description: BruceDropEmOff, born Bruce Ray Condones on 23 September 2000 in Riverdale, Georgia, is an American Twitch streamer and YouTuber known for reaction, Just Chatting and gaming broadcasts to his DEO community. He has said he began streaming at thirteen in 2013; his Twitch channel was created in 2015 and he streamed regularly from late 2016, first around NBA 2K and later across games including Grand Theft Auto V, Minecraft, Fortnite and Roblox. In 2022 he joined the Austin-based content organization One True King (OTK), and he left on 25 January 2023 after about ten months. After Twitch suspensions in early 2023, including an indefinite ban for ban evasion that was reversed after about a month, he moved to Kick, then announced his return to Twitch on 31 May 2024. After a hiatus from December 2024, he returned with a livestream on 13 September 2025, and he was still streaming in September and October 2026.

name: Britt Stewart
aliases: Britt Benae Stewart; Britt Stewart Durant
description: Britt Benae Stewart, born 21 September 1989 in Aurora, Colorado, is an American professional dancer, choreographer and teacher. She began ballet and tap classes at age three in Seattle, trained at the Artistic Fusion Dance Academy and the Denver School of the Arts, and briefly attended Loyola Marymount University before leaving to work professionally. As a teenager she was a principal dancer in the High School Musical films, and her commercial career later included Fame, Teen Beach Movie and tours and television performances with major recording artists. Stewart joined Dancing with the Stars as a troupe member in 2016 and, in August 2020, was named the first Black female professional dancer in the show's history. She reached the semifinals with Johnny Weir in her first season as a pro and recorded her best finish, fifth place, with Daniel Durant in 2022. She is president of Share the Movement, a nonprofit supporting young BIPOC dancers, and remains a Dancing with the Stars pro, competing with Taylor Hanson in the 2026 season.

name: Brandon Armstrong
description: Brandon Kelly Armstrong, born 5 June 1994 in San Francisco, California, is an American professional Latin and ballroom dancer and choreographer. Half African American and half Polynesian, he was adopted at birth, raised in Napa, California, and moved to Lehi, Utah, where he began dancing at twelve and trained with Corky, Shirley and Mark Ballas. After high school he served a two-year mission for the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. Armstrong joined Dancing with the Stars as a troupe member in season 24 and became a professional partner in season 27, paired with singer Tinashe. His breakthrough came in season 33, when he and actress Chandler Kinney became the first Black couple in the show's history to reach the finale, finishing third on 26 November 2024 with the season's highest cumulative judges' points and its first perfect score. He has since competed with Lauren Jauregui in season 34 and with Ciara Miller in season 35, and is married to Brylee Armstrong.

name: Bush Mama
description: Bush Mama is a 1979 American film by Ethiopian-American director Haile Gerima, a signal work of the L.A. Rebellion, the movement of political and experimental Black cinema that developed around the University of California, Los Angeles, in the 1970s. Gerima made the film as his thesis project at UCLA, directing, producing and editing it on a small budget, with cinematography by Roderick Young and Charles Burnett. It follows Dorothy, played by Barbara O. Jones, a mother living in the Watts neighborhood of Los Angeles, as she grapples with the imprisonment of her husband T.C., a discharged Vietnam veteran falsely arrested for a crime he did not commit, and navigates the bureaucratic tangles of public assistance. The film blends narrative fiction, documentary, surrealism and political modernism: its first half uses a cinema verite style with heavy improvisation, while the second half moves toward a more agitprop approach, tracing Dorothy's political awakening. The film runs 97 minutes, in 16mm. In 2022 it was selected for preservation in the National Film Registry by the Library of Congress as culturally, historically or aesthetically significant.

name: B.A. Parker
description: B.A. Parker is an American writer and audio producer who co-hosts Code Switch, NPR's flagship podcast and radio program on race and identity. Brooklyn-based when her appointment was announced in 2022, she joined host Gene Demby as the program's second host, an expansion funded by a $600,000 Corporation for Public Broadcasting grant secured that April. She came to Code Switch from New York magazine's The Cut podcast, where she had been co-host and lead producer since August 2020. Before that she produced the Nancy podcast at WNYC Studios, worked on the Heavyweight podcast at Gimlet Media and on NPR's Invisibilia, and contributed to This American Life. Public-media station WFYI, presenting her in Indianapolis in November 2022, also credits her career as a film professor. Announcing the appointment, Code Switch executive producer Steve Drummond praised her flair for language and her passion for deeply reported, sound-rich stories told with humor and compassion; Parker herself called the show a necessary beacon for people of color. Episode transcripts show her still introducing herself as a Code Switch host in December 2025, co-presenting the program's History Class series with Demby at the end of that year.

name: Black Mitzvah
description: Black Mitzvah is the 2019 Netflix stand-up comedy special by Tiffany Haddish, released on December 3, 2019 — her fortieth birthday, and the day she herself became a bat mitzvah. The Jewish Women's Archive records that the special turns on Haddish discovering her Jewish identity at twenty-seven, after reconnecting with her estranged father, an Eritrean Jew, and learning of the persecution he faced; on the day of release she read from the Torah in a ceremony led by Rabbi Susan Silverman. The Milken Institute's speaker biography likewise identifies the work as her 2019 Netflix comedy special, in which she reflects on her life, her fame, and the heritage she had only come to know as an adult. The recording of the special went on to win the Grammy Award for Best Comedy Album at the 63rd Annual Grammy Awards in 2021, as the Recording Academy's own artist record confirms. The Milken biography adds the historical weight of that win: Haddish became the second Black woman ever to win the category, and the first since Whoopi Goldberg won in 1986. The work is filed here as a comedy special — a filmed stand-up performance that also circulates, and won its Grammy, as an album.

name: Boogie Down Productions
description: Boogie Down Productions (BDP) was a Bronx hip-hop group formed by MC KRS-One (Kris Parker) and DJ Scott La Rock (Scott Sterling), who met in 1985 at a Bronx homeless shelter where Sterling worked as a social worker and Parker was living. AllMusic's biography records that the two became friends and decided to form a rap group, releasing the independent single 'Crack Attack' in 1986 and the debut album Criminal Minded on B-Boy Records in 1987. The Boombox's thirtieth-anniversary account gives the album's release as March 3, 1987, and describes its bare-bones production, its Bridge Wars battle with MC Shan and the Juice Crew, and tracks including 'South Bronx' and 'The Bridge Is Over.' AllMusic credits BDP as pioneers of both hardcore and political rap, and among the first hip-hop artists to incorporate Jamaican dancehall and ragga elements into their style. Months after the debut album, Scott La Rock was shot and killed in the Bronx; KRS-One continued Boogie Down Productions as a tribute to him, turning toward socially conscious material on By All Means Necessary (1988) and founding the Stop the Violence Movement, before retiring the BDP name in the early 1990s to record under his own.

name: Benjamin Hooks
aliases: Benjamin L. Hooks; Benjamin Lawson Hooks
description: Benjamin Hooks was a Memphis-born lawyer, Baptist minister, and civil-rights leader who led the NAACP as its executive director from 1977 to 1992. Born on January 31, 1925, he attended LeMoyne College, transferred to Howard University, served in the Army guarding Italian prisoners of war, graduated from Howard in 1944, and earned his law degree at DePaul University in Chicago in 1948 after no Tennessee law school would admit him. Returning to Memphis, he practiced law, joined the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, and was ordained a Baptist minister in 1956. In 1965 he became the first African American to serve on Tennessee's criminal court bench. In 1972 he became the first African American member of the Federal Communications Commission. He left the FCC to lead the NAACP, and after retiring taught at Fisk University as a professor of social justice. He died on April 15, 2010, having received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2007.

name: Benjamin O. Davis Jr.
description: Benjamin O. Davis Jr. was a U.S. Air Force general who commanded the Tuskegee Airmen in World War II. Born in Washington, D.C., on December 18, 1912, the son of Benjamin O. Davis Sr., he entered West Point in 1932 as its first Black cadet of the twentieth century, was shunned by classmates for four years, and graduated in 1936 in the top fifth of his class. Barred from flying units, he served in the infantry before earning his wings in March 1942 and taking command of the 99th Fighter Squadron, the first all-Black unit in the Army Air Forces, and then the 332nd Fighter Group in Italy. His airmen flew thousands of sorties and built the escort record that helped dismantle the case for a segregated military. Davis helped integrate the Air Force, became its first Black general after his success commanding an integrated fighter wing in Korea, retired in 1970, and was advanced to four-star general by President Bill Clinton in 1998. He died on July 4, 2002, and is buried at Arlington National Cemetery.

name: Benjamin E. Mays
aliases: Benjamin Elijah Mays; Dr. Benjamin E. Mays
description: Benjamin Elijah Mays (1894–1984) was a Baptist minister and educator who served as president of Morehouse College in Atlanta from 1940 to 1967 and became one of the most influential mentors of the civil rights generation. Born on August 1, 1894, in Epworth, South Carolina, to parents who had been enslaved, he earned his B.A. from Bates College in 1920, was ordained a Baptist minister in 1921, and completed his M.A. and Ph.D. at the University of Chicago. From 1934 to 1940 he was dean of the School of Religion at Howard University. At Morehouse his weekly chapel addresses drew students into sustained discussion of theology and public life; Martin Luther King Jr., a student there in the 1940s, regarded him as a spiritual mentor and intellectual father, and Mays delivered the eulogy at King's funeral in 1968. After retiring from Morehouse, Mays became the first Black president of the Atlanta Board of Education. He received the NAACP's Spingarn Medal and, by the Stanford King Institute's count, 28 honorary degrees. He died in Atlanta on March 28, 1984.

name: Black Harvest Film Festival
description: The Black Harvest Film Festival is Chicago's annual showcase for films that celebrate, explore, and share the Black, African American, and African Diaspora experience, presented by the Gene Siskel Film Center of the School of the Art Institute of Chicago since 1994. This is a Chicago record: the festival was created to answer a cultural need in Chicago, in the words of its longtime programming leadership, and it remains centered on Chicago premieres, local filmmakers, and community programming alongside international Black cinema. Its 30th annual edition ran in person at the Film Center from November 8 to 21, 2024, curated by Jada-Amina and Nick Leffel. The festival's 20th edition ran August 1–28, 2014, with a strong slate of Chicago-made work. Following the death in 2022 of co-founder and consultant Sergio Mims, the Film Center established the Sergio Mims Fund for Black Excellence in Filmmaking to support the next generation of Black filmmakers. Across three decades the festival has functioned as the Midwest's principal theatrical home for Black independent film.

name: Black Music Month
aliases: African-American Music Appreciation Month; Black Music Appreciation Month; National Black Music Month
description: Black Music Month is the annual June observance celebrating the African American musical influences that the Smithsonian's National Museum of African American History and Culture calls an essential part of the nation's cultural heritage. It originated in 1979, when Philadelphia soul pioneer Kenny Gamble, Cleveland radio DJ Ed Wright, and media strategist Dyana Williams brought the idea forth out of the Black Music Association, which Gamble had founded in 1978 on the model of the Country Music Association. On June 7, 1979, President Jimmy Carter designated June as the month to recognize Black music, and the first celebration was held on the White House lawn. The founders' original purpose was economic as much as celebratory: to promote, protect, and perpetuate the business of Black music. The observance is re-established annually by presidential proclamation; under President Barack Obama it was renamed African-American Music Appreciation Month, a name later set aside in favor of the original. Each June, museums, media, and the music industry mark the genres Black artists created and fostered, from spirituals and gospel through blues, jazz, R&B, rock and roll, and hip-hop.

name: Blanche K. Bruce
description: Blanche Kelso Bruce (1841–1898) was a Republican United States senator from Mississippi during Reconstruction and the first African American to serve a full term in the U.S. Senate. Born into slavery on March 1, 1841, near Farmville, Virginia, he was educated by the tutor hired for his enslaver's son and fled to freedom in Kansas at the start of the Civil War. He taught school in Missouri, organizing a school for Black children in Hannibal in 1864, then moved to Mississippi in 1869, where he became a planter and rose through Bolivar County offices, including sheriff and tax collector. Mississippi's legislature elected him to the Senate on February 4, 1874; he served from March 1875 to March 1881 as the second African American senator, after Hiram Revels. In the Senate he defended the rights of freedpeople and other minorities, and on February 14, 1879, he became the first Black senator to preside over a Senate session. Afterward he served twice as Register of the Treasury, from 1881 and again from 1897, and as recorder of deeds for the District of Columbia. He died in Washington, D.C., on March 17, 1898.

name: Barbara Jordan
description: Barbara Charline Jordan was an American lawyer, educator, and Democratic politician born in Houston, Texas, on February 21, 1936. She graduated from Phillis Wheatley High School in 1952, earned a B.A. from Texas Southern University in 1956, and received her law degree from Boston University School of Law in 1959. Admitted to the Massachusetts and Texas bars that year, she began practicing law in Houston in 1960. Elected to the Texas Senate in 1966, she served from 1967 to 1972 as the first Black woman in that body and the first African American elected to it since Reconstruction. In 1972 she won a Houston-based seat in the U.S. House of Representatives, and she served in the 93rd, 94th, and 95th Congresses, from January 3, 1973, to January 3, 1979. As a freshman representative she sat on the House Judiciary Committee during its impeachment investigation of President Richard M. Nixon, and her opening statement on the constitutional gravity of the process made her a national figure; the committee passed three articles of impeachment. After Congress she taught at the Lyndon B. Johnson School of Public Affairs at the University of Texas at Austin and chaired the U.S. Commission on Immigration Reform. She died in Austin on January 17, 1996.

name: Bert Williams
description: Egbert Austin Williams, known as Bert Williams, was a Bahamian-born American comedian and singer born on November 12, 1874, in Nassau, Bahamas. His family moved to the United States when he was ten, settling in Riverside, California. In San Francisco in 1893 he began working with George Walker in minstrel companies, and the pair developed a double act in which Walker played a fast-talking city hustler and Williams, in blackface, played a slow-witted, woeful bumbler. They reached New York in 1896, added a cakewalk finale at Koster and Bial's, and began recording for the Victor label in 1901. Their In Dahomey, which premiered on Broadway on February 18, 1903, was the first fully realized musical comedy performed by an all-Black company; it toured England and played a command performance at Buckingham Palace. Williams composed more than seventy songs, among them "Nobody," introduced in 1905. Walker retired from the stage in February 1909 because of illness and died in January 1911. Williams then joined Florenz Ziegfeld's Follies in 1910 and was its star attraction for some eight seasons. He became a United States citizen in 1918 and died in New York City on March 4, 1922.

name: Bernice Johnson Reagon
aliases: Bernice Johnson; Dr. Bernice Johnson Reagon
description: Bernice Johnson Reagon, born October 4, 1942, in Albany, Georgia, was an American singer, composer, scholar, and civil rights activist. The daughter of a Baptist minister, she entered Albany State College in 1959 and became a student leader in the Albany Movement. Arrested in 1961 for joining a Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee demonstration, she was expelled from Albany State and joined the Freedom Singers, the Albany-based group that toured the country raising money for SNCC's civil rights campaigns. She completed her B.A. in history at Spelman College in 1970 and earned a Ph.D. in United States history from Howard University in 1975. In 1973 she founded Sweet Honey in the Rock, an a cappella ensemble of African American women whose repertoire joined gospel, blues, and African traditions to songs of social witness; she composed and produced much of its repertoire and led the group for three decades. From 1974 she worked at the Smithsonian Institution as a folklorist, program director, and curator, and was named curator emeritus in 1993. She received a MacArthur Foundation fellowship in 1989 and created Wade in the Water, the Peabody Award-winning Smithsonian and National Public Radio series on African American sacred music traditions, in 1994. She died on July 16, 2024, aged eighty-one.

name: Black Swan Records
aliases: Black Swan; Black Swan Phonograph Company; Pace Phonograph Corporation
description: Black Swan Records was a Harlem record company founded in 1921 by music publisher Harry Pace as the record division of his Pace Phonograph Corporation. It was the first Black-owned recording company to sell popular music to Black audiences nationally, and the first company to record Black classical musicians as well as blues and jazz artists. Pace named the label for the nineteenth-century concert singer Elizabeth Taylor Greenfield, known as the Black Swan, and its board of directors included Bert Williams, Lester Walton, and W. E. B. Du Bois. The label's first recording appeared in May 1921, and its first hit was Ethel Waters's Down Home Blues, released the same month. Fletcher Henderson worked as recording director and assembled the backing bands, William Grant Still arranged and directed music, and James P. Johnson recorded some of his first solos for the label. In 1922 Pace entered an arrangement with the white-owned Olympic Disc Record Corporation as larger white-owned companies moved into the market for Black artists. Black Swan released more than 180 records before Pace declared bankruptcy in December 1923. Paramount Records bought the catalog in March 1924 and issued records under the Black Swan name until December 1924.

name: Bonnie Lee
aliases: Jessie Lee Frealls; Bonnie "Bombshell" Lane; Bonnie Lee Murray; The Sweetheart of the Blues
description: Bonnie Lee, born Jessie Lee Frealls on June 11, 1931, in Bunkie, Louisiana, and raised in Beaumont, Texas, was an American Chicago blues singer known as the Sweetheart of the Blues. She studied piano and sang in her church choir as a child, toured the South as a teenager with the Famous Georgia Minstrels, and relocated to Chicago in 1958, working as a singer and dancer. In 1960 she signed with J. Mayo Williams's Ebony label and cut her debut single, Sad and Evil Woman, credited against her wishes to Bonnie Bombshell Lane. After the single failed and family obligations interrupted her career, she resurfaced in 1967 alongside pianist Sunnyland Slim, opening for him for years and holding residencies at North Side clubs including Wise Fools, B.L.U.E.S., and Blue Chicago. She recorded singles for Slim's Airway label in the late 1970s, toured Europe in 1982 with Zora Young and Big Time Sarah as Blues with the Girls, and then worked for a decade with bassist Willie Kent, singing regularly at B.L.U.E.S. with his band. Her albums under her own name were Sweetheart of the Blues (Delmark, 1995) and I'm Good (1998). She died in Chicago on September 7, 2006, aged seventy-five.

name: Bethune-Cookman University
aliases: B-CU; Bethune-Cookman College; Daytona-Cookman Collegiate Institute; Daytona Literary and Industrial Training School for Negro Girls; Daytona Educational and Industrial Training School for Negro Girls; Daytona Normal and Industrial Institute for Negro Girls
description: Bethune-Cookman University is a historically Black university in Daytona Beach, Florida, founded by educator Mary McLeod Bethune. On October 3, 1904, Bethune opened a training school for Negro girls with $1.50, faith, five little girls, and her son Albert, in the account given on the university's own history page. The school grew through several stages during Bethune's lifetime. In 1923 it merged with the Cookman Institute of Jacksonville, founded in 1872 and described by the university as the first institution of higher education for Black people in Florida; the merger was finalized in 1925 as the Daytona-Cookman Collegiate Institute and brought a Methodist affiliation. On April 27, 1931, the name was officially changed to Bethune-Cookman College. The university states that it achieved university status in 2007, after adding a graduate program in transformational leadership. It describes itself today in terms of its HBCU sensibility, small-university community, and Bethune's legacy of service, and it reports more than 19,000 graduates since 1943. Its best-known predecessor alumnus is labor and civil-rights leader A. Philip Randolph, valedictorian of Cookman Institute's 1907 class.

name: Black Perspectives
description: Black Perspectives is the Chicago International Film Festival's program devoted to Black American cinema and films of the African diaspora, founded in 1997 in collaboration with Spike Lee and presented by Cinema/Chicago. The festival states the program's purpose as highlighting the excellence and diversity of Black American cinema and diaspora filmmaking; across three decades it has premiered Ava DuVernay's first feature and presented work by Barry Jenkins, Maya Angelou, Djibril Diop Mambéty, Abderrahmane Sissako and Steve McQueen, and the festival has honored Viola Davis, Forest Whitaker, Sidney Poitier, Halle Berry, Morgan Freeman and Pam Grier in the program's history. The program now runs year-round. Its 30th anniversary anchored the 62nd festival in October 2026: a Career Achievement Award evening for Marlon Wayans at the Logan Center on October 19, moderated by Omar Epps; Cheryl Dunye's Career Achievement tribute with a retrospective screening of The Watermelon Woman; Aunjanue Ellis-Taylor's Tour de Force Award at the world premiere of Liz Here Now; Sophie Okonedo's Spotlight Award at the Centerpiece presentation of Mouse; new work by Ava DuVernay (14th) and David Greaves (Once Upon a Time in Harlem); a twelve-feature slate spanning the United States, France, Senegal, Rwanda, Haiti and Brazil; and a seven-film shorts program, Love With No Place to Go.

name: Brittany Winstead
description: Brittany Winstead, PharmD, RPh, is Associate Director, Program Management — Solid Tumor at AbbVie, the biopharmaceutical company headquartered in North Chicago, Illinois; AbbVie's own site identifies her in that role and as Global Chair of its Black Business Network employee resource group. WVON's roster renders her title in the form 'Associate Director, R&D Oncology' (solid tumor being AbbVie's oncology program area). She was named to WVON's 40 Under 40 Game Changers Class of 2026.
